Best NAS for Jellyfin 2026: Hardware Transcoding — ubnas Skip to content Free NAS calculators and guides for self-hosting and homelabs Free NAS calculators & guides Try the RAID & ZFS capacity calculator → 
 Topic NAS Guides 
 Published Jul 1, 2026 
 Updated Oct 13, 2026 
 Written by ubnas 
 Reading time 6 min 
 For smooth Jellyfin hardware transcoding you want an Intel chip with Quick Sync (an integrated GPU). In 2026 the easiest turnkey picks are UGreen's NASync boxes — the 2-bay DXP2800 (Intel N100) and the 4-bay DXP4800 Plus (Intel Pentium Gold 8505). If you're comfortable with a little setup, a cheap Intel N100/N150 mini-PC running your Jellyfin server is the best value of all. Avoid AMD-based Synology models — and note that Synology's newest units disable hardware transcoding entirely.
 How we sourced this: built from manufacturer specs, independent reviews and current data — not paid placement. Where our guidance is based on published data rather than our own bench testing, we say so. See How we test . Some links may be affiliate links — see our disclosure . 
 Fig. 1 Comparison of Jellyfin workloads showing what hardware direct play, 1080p transcoding and 4K HDR transcoding require 
 The one spec that matters: Intel Quick Sync
 Jellyfin only has to work hard when it transcodes — that is, when it re-encodes your video on the fly because a client can't play the original file, the bitrate is too high for the connection, or subtitles need to be burned in. If every device could direct-play, a Raspberry Pi would do. But the moment a 4K HEVC HDR file has to become 1080p H.264 for a phone or a smart TV, you need a hardware encoder, or the CPU melts trying to do it in software.
 Intel's built-in hardware encoder is called Quick Sync Video (QSV) , and it lives inside the integrated GPU on most Intel chips. It's the reason a modest, low-power Intel NAS can push several simultaneous 4K transcodes while barely warming up. Jellyfin's own hardware-selection guide ranks Intel iGPUs highly for transcoding and explicitly discourages AMD, citing "poor encoder quality and poor driver support." Intel iGPUs from 7th-gen Kaby Lake and Gemini Lake onward decode and encode 10-bit HEVC, and Jellyfin supports HDR-to-SDR tone-mapping on every Intel GPU with 10-bit HEVC decoding, which is exactly what you need for a modern 4K library.
 Two practical rules follow from this:
 Buy Intel with an iGPU. Quick Sync is the whole game for a transcoding media server.
 Give it enough RAM. Jellyfin's docs recommend at least 8GB for a typical deployment; a single 4K transcode can eat a big chunk of a 4GB buffer.
 If you're still deciding between media servers, see Jellyfin vs Plex . Ready to build? Our how to set up Jellyfin guide walks through the Docker install.
 The picks
 We haven't bench-tested every unit here ourselves; the guidance below is built from manufacturer specs, the Jellyfin project's own documentation, and independent reviews, which we cite in Sources. Prices move constantly, so we link retailers rather than quote figures that go stale.

 Why the DIY mini-PC keeps winning. The Intel N100 is rated at a 6W TDP, and independent testing shows the N100's iGPU comfortably handling multiple concurrent 4K HEVC transcodes — reviewers report three or more 4K streams, and many more at 1080p. XDA built a capable 4K Quick Sync Jellyfin box for well under $200. You lose the tidy NAS chassis and drive bays, but you gain the best price-to-performance ratio in the whole category. Pair it with a separate NAS or a couple of drives, and you have a fantastic setup.
 Why UGreen for a real NAS. UGreen's NASync line puts genuine Quick Sync silicon in a proper multi-bay enclosure. The DXP2800 uses the Intel N100 (the same well-liked chip as the DIY route) with 8GB DDR5 and 2.5GbE; the DXP4800 Plus steps up to the 12th-gen Pentium Gold 8505, 8GB DDR5, and 10GbE plus 2.5GbE networking. Both run Docker, which is how you'll deploy Jellyfin.
 The AMD-Synology trap (and a newer Synology problem)
 This is the mistake that sends people back to the return counter. Synology's Plus models have split into Intel and AMD lines, and the AMD ones cannot hardware-transcode. 
 The AMD Ryzen models — DS925+, DS923+, DS725+ — use chips (Ryzen V1500B / R1600) with no integrated GPU . No iGPU means no hardware encoder. They're fine for storage and direct-play, but a single software 4K transcode will bring them to their knees. Do not buy one expecting a smooth Jellyfin transcoding experience.
 The Intel models in the 2025 refresh — DS225+, DS425+ — do use the Quick Sync-capable Celeron J4125. But there's a catch: on 2025-and-later models Synology quietly removed the kernel graphics driver that Plex, Jellyfin and Emby rely on, so hardware transcoding no longer works out of the box even where the CPU supports it. Community SSH workarounds exist, but that's not something we'd recommend most buyers depend on.
 The older Intel units ( DS224+, DS423+ ) still transcode via Quick Sync on current DSM, so an existing or used one is fine. But for a new purchase in 2026, Synology is no longer the obvious Jellyfin choice it once was. For the wider brand comparison, see Synology vs UGreen vs QNAP vs TrueNAS .
 Decision guide
 You want the cheapest thing that transcodes 4K well → Intel N100/N150 mini-PC running Jellyfin in Docker. Add storage separately.
 You want a real NAS and Jellyfin in one box, 2 drives → UGreen DXP2800 (N100).
 Bigger library, more simultaneous streams, faster networking → UGreen DXP4800 Plus (Pentium 8505, 10GbE).
 You love a polished NAS app store → an Intel-based ASUSTOR (verify the model's CPU supports Quick Sync before buying).
 You already own a DS224+/DS423+ → keep it; it transcodes fine today.
 You were about to buy a DS925+/DS923+/DS725+ for Jellyfin → don't. No iGPU, no hardware transcoding.
 Once you've picked drives, our RAID capacity calculator helps you plan usable space, and it's worth setting up cloud backup for your NAS before you fill it with an irreplaceable library. Building a Plex box instead? See best NAS for Plex .
 FAQ
 Do I actually need hardware transcoding for Jellyfin? 
Only if clients can't direct-play your files. If every device plays your formats natively over a fast local network, almost any NAS works. But burned-in subtitles, high-bitrate 4K over the internet, and older TVs all force transcoding — and that's when Quick Sync saves you.
 Is an Intel N100 really enough for 4K? 
Yes, for most homes. Independent testing shows the N100's Quick Sync engine handling multiple concurrent 4K HEVC transcodes and many more 1080p streams. It only struggles if you throw a large number of simultaneous 4K tone-mapping jobs at it.
 Why is AMD such a problem for transcoding? 
Two reasons. Synology's AMD chips have no iGPU at all, so there's no hardware encoder. And even where AMD GPUs exist, Jellyfin's own docs rate AMD's encoder quality and driver support as the weakest of the major options. Intel Quick Sync is simply the safer bet.
 Can I use Jellyfin on any Synology? 
You can install it, but hardware transcoding depends on the model: older Intel units (DS224+/DS423+) do it, AMD units can't, and 2025+ models have the transcoding driver removed. Check the exact model before buying.
 How much RAM should I get? 
Jellyfin recommends at least 8GB for a typical deployment. It's cheap insurance, and both UGreen boxes above ship with 8GB DDR5.
 Define your Jellyfin workload before buying
 List each client, its supported codecs, remote bandwidth and the maximum simultaneous streams. Direct play needs little CPU; subtitle burn-in, HDR tone mapping and codec conversion can trigger a full transcode. Jellyfin's official documentation supports several GPU families, so Intel Quick Sync is a practical default rather than the only possible solution. Test with your hardest real file before scaling a purchase recommendation.

Hardware Selection | Jellyfin 
 Skip to main content 
 On this page 
 The following is intended to help you choose appropriate hardware for a Jellyfin server and take full advantage of its features (e.g. hardware acceleration).
 Simple Guide ​ 
 Below is a list of recommended specs to run Jellyfin. Whilst Jellyfin can work on relatively low-end hardware, the following specs are recommended for a good experience.
 Shared Items ​ 
 Some component recommendations do not change regardless of the hardware configuration:
 Storage: 100GB SSD for your OS, Jellyfin files and transcoding cache. 1 Consider adding more on Windows 11, or if you have many large media files that need transcoding.
 Networking: Gigabit Ethernet Adapter or faster, WiFi or Powerline not recommended.
 Internet Connection: At least 20 Mbps upload bandwidth for remote access. 2 
 1 Your largest media file times the max number of concurrent streams all your users will consume can be used as a rule of thumb for the transcoding file size. 
 2 If you have less than 100 Mbps of total upload bandwidth, a bandwidth limit of 70% of your upload speed for Jellyfin is recommended to avoid affecting internet usage outside of Jellyfin. This option can be found in the Jellyfin Server Dashboard .
 Hardware Encoder Quality ​ 
 Different vendors have different hardware encoder implementations and produce different results. Usually, newer generations within the same vendor will provide better results. The following is a quick comparison on the quality between vendors on modern products.
 NVIDIA (RTX 50) ≥ Intel (Arc-B) ≥ Apple ≥ Intel ≥ NVIDIA ≥ AMD ≥ AMD H.264 (RX 9000) >>> AMD H.264 * 
 * This only represents the default Jellyfin settings. The quality may be different depending on your exact configuration.
 Server with Integrated Graphics ​ 
 If you do not intend to use a dedicated graphics card, the following specs are recommended:
 CPU: Intel Core i5-11400, Intel Pentium Gold G7400, Intel N100, Apple M series or newer (excluding Intel J/M/N/Y series up to 11th gen)
 RAM: 8GB System RAM (Consider adding more on Windows 11)
 Graphics: Intel UHD 710, Apple M series or newer
 AMD is NOT recommended if you intend to use integrated graphics for Jellyfin.
 caution
 Intel 7-10th gen CPUs have been removed from this list, since the toolkit for these generations has been deprecated by Intel. If you own a 7-10th gen CPU with integrated graphics, please continue to use them for Jellyfin, as they are still perfectly capable of performing the task. If you are making a purchase decision, you may wish to consider alternatives.
 Server with Dedicated Graphics ​ 
 If you intend to use a dedicated graphics card (including upgrading an old system with a dedicated GPU), the following specs are recommended:
 CPU: Intel Core i5-2300，AMD FX-8100 or better (Geekbench 6 Multicore 1500 or better), CPU Vendor / Performance will NOT affect hardware encode speed or quality
 RAM: 8GB. (4GB may be sufficient for a Linux server without its own GUI.)
 Graphics: Intel Arc A series or newer, NVIDIA GTX16/RTX20 series or newer (Excluding GTX1650), AMD is NOT recommended .
 Intel Drivers are much easier to install on Linux, with many distributions including them by default. If you do not need CUDA for other applications, it is highly recommended that you stick with Intel Graphics on Linux.
 caution
 Intel ARC B-series cards require ReBar to be enabled. This means you must use it on a platform with Intel 10th gen, AMD Ryzen 3000 series or newer. Intel ARC A-series cards do not require ReBar to function, however, ReBar should be enabled for optimal performance.
 Servers without GPUs ​ 
 Not having a GPU is NOT recommended for Jellyfin, as video transcoding on the CPU is very performance demanding. HDR
to SDR tone-mapping can make the situation even worse. Depending on your configuration, you may end up in situations
where a Ryzen 9 5950X cannot handle even a single video stream. Please read the section below for more details 
 Low Power Servers ​ 
 For users with expensive electricity, or running battery-powered servers:
 Intel 12th gen or above N series platforms
 Apple M Series Mac mini
 Rockchip RK3588 / RK3588S SBC ( Advanced Users Only )
 Potentially Problematic Hardware ​ 
 These hardware platforms might lead to a poor Jellyfin experience. Please be careful to avoid them when shopping for hardware.
 Intel "Atom" CPUs: Intel J/M/N/Y series low power CPUs up to 11th gen use a different architecture than higher end parts, leading to subpar performance despite what their names might suggest. It is advised to avoid using these parts in a Jellyfin Server.
 Prebuilt NAS Appliances: The software environment on most prebuilt NAS appliances often makes third-party software more challenging to install, sometimes even preventing it from working properly despite a successful installation. They may have low-end processors that are too slow for an acceptable Jellyfin experience. (e.g. Intel Atom, Realtek ARM CPUs, etc.).
 Most Single Board Computers (SBC): Most SBCs (including the Raspberry Pi, especially the Raspberry Pi 5 ) are too slow to provide an acceptable Jellyfin experience as they often lack proper support for hardware acceleration. If you really want to run Jellyfin on an SBC, you may wish to consider models based on the following platforms: Rockchip RK3588 / RK3588S, Intel Core, Intel 12th gen N series
 AMD Graphics: AMD Graphics have poor encoder quality and poor driver support. This applies even on Linux .
 Low-end GPUs: Certain low-end GPUs (e.g. GT1030, RX6400) are not capable of hardware encoding. These models cannot be used for hardware acceleration for a Jellyfin Server.
 Very old X86 CPUs: Starting with Jellyfin 10.11, X86 CPUs that support the SSE4.1 instruction set is a requirement. For Intel, Penryn (Q4 2007) and newer support SSE4.1. For AMD, Bulldozer (Q4 2011) and newer support SSE4.1.
 Detailed Guide ​ 
 CPU ​ 
 The CPU will be responsible for many tasks, notably:
 Transcoding Audio
 Decoding video in unsupported codecs
 Whilst most audio codecs will only utilize a single core, they are very lightweight and most CPUs should be able to handle them without issues. (e.g. a Ryzen 5950X transcoding FLAC -> AAC runs at ~110x real-time.)
 Video in unsupported codecs are usually older formats that are easier to decode. Assuming hardware acceleration is properly configured, any modern CPU with 4 threads should be able to handle the workload.
 However, newer codecs can also require software decoding if there are no available hardware decoders. HEVC, VP9 and AV1 can be VERY demanding even on modern CPUs if hardware acceleration is not available on a Jellyfin Server. This is why a hardware platform capable of HEVC 10bit hardware decoding is strongly recommended.
 In our custom jellyfin-ffmpeg fork, the dav1d decoder is enabled, leading to faster software decoding compared to HEVC or VP9. However, it will still use significantly more resources compared to software decoding H.264 and older codecs. Since we have a more efficient AV1 software decoder, and AV1 media isn't common yet, you shouldn't worry about AV1 when choosing components for your Jellyfin Server.
 Integrated Graphics ​ 
 Integrated graphics can be useful for transcoding video. For more information, please refer to the GPU section .
 Resizable BAR ​ 
 Resizable Bar (ReBAR) is a PCI Express feature that optimizes access to PCIe devices. This feature requires support from both the platform and the device. Support for this feature is respectively available beginning with Intel 10th gen and AMD Ryzen 3000 Series.
 In BIOS settings of motherboards, it may also be called Smart Access Memory or Clever Access Memory 
 When using Intel ARC Graphics, Resizable BAR is recommended. Disabling it will result in a 10% reduction in transcoding performance. However, given how fast the media engine on Intel ARC is, this should not be a problem for the average deployment.
 Software HDR to SDR Tone-mapping ​ 
 If there is no GPU available on a Jellyfin Server, the CPU can also be used to tone-map HDR content to SDR. This can be very demanding on
the CPU, therefore a GPU is ALWAYS recommended. When using software tone-mapping, a software encoder will always be
used. Tone-mapping 4K 60fps Dolby Vision content to 4K 60fps H264 SDR requires a Ryzen 9 5950X for faster than real-time
transcoding. You may find current desktop CPUs do not offer adequate performance if you seek to provide streams in H.265 or AV1.
 System Memory (RAM) ​ 
 As a general recommendation, at least 8GB is recommended for the average deployment. For a Linux server running without a GUI, 4GB may be enough.
 It is recommended to add more memory when using Windows 11 due to the OS being heavier.
 Graphics Cards (GPUs) ​ 
 note
 The quality of transcoded video is highly dependent on the target codecs used by your client and your GPU architecture. Make sure you have verified them so you can choose the GPU best suited for your use case.
 With modern systems, the media engines are usually located on the GPUs. Therefore, the available hardware acceleration options are determined by the choice of GPU.
 Encoder Quality: NVIDIA (RTX 50) ≥ Intel (Arc-B) ≥ Apple ≥ Intel ≥ NVIDIA ≥ AMD ≥ AMD H.264 (RX 9000) >>> AMD H.264 * 
 * This only represents the default Jellyfin settings. The quality may be different depending on your exact configuration.
 NVIDIA Blackwell (RTX 50) NVENC represents the state of the art in hardware encoder quality. It introduces more optimized encoding tools, allowing it to deliver significant quality gains over its predecessor, Ada (RTX 40), and even Intel Arc Battlemage. The most visible difference is that Intel's encoder is more likely to produce blocky artifacts when processing dark details.
 Intel is always recommended on non-Apple hardware for the following reasons:
 Intel provides a good quality encoder, slightly better than pre-Blackwell NVIDIA and significantly better than AMD H.264.
 Intel drivers and the compute environment is much easier to setup than NVIDIA.
 AMD is the least preferred choice due to its sub-par H.264 encoders prior to RDNA4 (RX 9000). While its H.265 (HEVC) and AV1 encoders offer noticeable improvements, they still lag behind Intel and NVIDIA. Since the average Jellyfin client relies heavily on H.264 hardware decoding, you will inevitably transcode to H.264 most of the time, making AMD's weakness a major bottleneck.
 A list of common codecs can be found in the codec support documentation .
 The following is a list of video codecs Jellyfin supports transcoding to:
 H.264 (most common transcode target)
 H.265 (Jellyfin clients have limited support)
 AV1 (new in Jellyfin v10.9, supported by most modern browsers)
 A greater number of codecs is desirable for decoding support. With that said, media is generally available in a small number of codecs. The most important one to look for is HEVC 10bit decoding support, as decoding can be CPU intensive.
 Intel Graphics ​ 
 Please refer to this table for supported codecs.
 Intel CPUs with a model name that ends with F do not have integrated graphics. These are intended to be used with a dedicated graphics card, meaning that if you wish to use Intel integrated graphics, this is not an appropriate choice of component for your Jellyfin Server.
 If you intend to use Linux with Intel 12/13th gen integrated graphics or ARC, these GPUs only work on Linux Kernel 6.2 or newer. Please check your distribution to make sure it has a supported Linux Kernel version. Further information: Known Intel limitations on Linux .
 caution
 Intel 10th gen and older integrated graphics are losing support for QSV on Linux due to the SDK for these platforms being deprecated by Intel. If you own 7-10th gen CPUs with integrated graphics, please continue to use them for Jellyfin. If you are making a purchase decision, you may wish to consider a newer CPU if you plan on using Intel integrated graphics.
 NVIDIA Graphics ​ 
 Please refer to this table for supported codecs.
 Certain low-end cards (e.g. GT 1030) do not have encoding hardware. Please be careful when choosing a GPU.
 AMD Graphics ​ 
 AMD graphics are the least preferred choice for Jellyfin, this information is solely provided for reference. Further reading on AMD VCN & VCE supported codecs:
 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Core_Next 
 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Coding_Engine 
 Certain low-end cards (e.g., RX 6400, RX 6500) do not have encoding hardware. Please be careful when choosing a GPU.
 Many AMD CPUs do not have integrated graphics. These are intended to be used with a dedicated graphics card.
 For Ryzen 1000 - 5000 Series, only desktop CPUs with a model description that ends with G have integrated graphics—other Ryzen 1000-5000 desktop CPUs do NOT.
 For Ryzen 7000 Series, desktop CPUs with a model description that ends with F do NOT have integrated graphics, whereas the rest do.
 Please check the product page of your CPU for more info.
 Apple Silicon ​ 
 Supported codecs are listed below:
 Codec M1, M2 Family M3 Family 
 H.264 8bit ✅ ✅ 
 H.264 10bit 🔶 🔶 
 H.265 8bit ✅ ✅ 
 H.265 10bit ✅ ✅ 
 VP9 8bit 🔶 🔶 
 VP9 10bit 🔶 🔶 
 AV1 ❌ ❌ 1 
 ✅ = Encode + Decode, 🔶 = Decode Only, ❌ = Not Supported.
 1 Although the hardware does support AV1 decoding, ffmpeg does not yet support it .
 caution
 No Apple Silicon media engine drivers currently exist for non-macOS operating systems. You will NOT be able to use hardware acceleration if the server is running Asahi Linux .
 Rockchip VPU ​ 
 Currently only the VPU on RK3588/3588S SoC is recommended, which can handle most common video codecs, including AV1 decode.
 Supported codecs are listed below:
 Codec RK3588/3588S 
 MPEG1/2/4 8bit 🔶 
 VC1 8bit ❌ 
 H.264 8bit ✅ 
 H.264 10bit 🔶 
 H.265 8bit ✅ 
 H.265 10bit 🔶 
 VP8 8bit 🔶 
 VP9 8bit 🔶 
 VP9 10bit 🔶 
 AV1 🔶 
 ✅ = Encode + Decode, 🔶 = Decode Only, ❌ = Not Supported.
 Storage ​ 
 There are two general types of storage that can be used on a Jellyfin Server. Media files and Jellyfin files respectively require specific hardware to optimize performance.
 Media Storage ​ 
 Anything with higher sequential access speed than bitrate of media is acceptable. If desired, this storage may be a network share, or a cloud storage service mounted on the Jellyfin Server host.
 Jellyfin Files ​ 
 The files for Jellyfin itself (i.e., not your media files) will see a lot of random access, therefore SSDs are recommended for these files. AVOID mechanical drives that use SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) as they will result in a VERY poor experience.
 Networking ​ 
 Networking is for connecting your Jellyfin server to other devices. It is recommended that the Jellyfin Server be connected to your network via Ethernet cable for optimal performance. Wi-Fi or Powerline solutions for a Jellyfin Server are NOT recommended and will result in an especially poor experience.
 Jellyfin Server is not designed to be exposed directly to the internet. Ensure it remains protected behind a properly configured firewall or other secure network environment.

 ⓘ This post contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 A NAS without Intel QuickSync hands every stream your TV cannot play straight to the CPU. A four-core appliance gives up on the first 4K HDR file. That single spec decides the best NAS for Jellyfin more than bay count or brand, yet most spec sheets hide it behind phrases like “hardware transcoding engine”.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 169001 
 We narrowed the field to five boxes you can buy new on Amazon US today. Each chip was read against the Intel ARK spec pages and the Jellyfin hardware acceleration docs, including where Jellyfin support ends for Jasper Lake. Plex runs on all of them too, but a lifetime Plex Pass now costs $749.99, which is why Jellyfin leads this guide. This is a spec and capability guide, not a bench test: stock, prices and chip data were checked in October 2026 against the makers’ pages and live listings, so no stream count below is borrowed from an old benchmark.
 Top picks at a glance
 For most homes running Jellyfin or Plex, buy the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus . Its 12th-gen Intel chip has QuickSync with AV1 decode, it ships with 10GbE, and it takes any drive. Every pick in this table was in stock on Amazon US when we checked, and every one except the Synology transcodes in hardware.

 Best overall UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus Pentium Gold 8505 Yes, AV1 decode 4 + 2 M.2 about $630 to $660 
 Best value TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Intel N95 Yes, AV1 decode 4 + 3 M.2 about $510 
 Best budget UGREEN NASync DXP2800 Intel N100 Yes, AV1 decode 2 + 2 M.2 about $370 to $390 
 Best for Plex with PCIe QNAP TS-664 Celeron N5095 Yes, no AV1 6 + 2 M.2 about $800 
 Best for DSM Synology DS925+ AMD Ryzen V1500B No iGPU 4 + 2 M.2 about $770 
 Two picks from the last version of this page are gone. The TerraMaster F4-425 Pro with the Core i3-N305 is out of stock, and its N350 replacement sells for about $800, more than the UGREEN four-bay with built-in 10GbE, so it no longer earns a value award. The eight-bay UGREEN DXP8800 Plus is also out of stock on Amazon, and our 8-bay NAS guide covers the large-library boxes you can still buy.
 How we picked these boxes
 None of these units sat in our rack for a month of streaming, and we will not pretend otherwise. Competing guides quote “10 simultaneous 4K streams” figures lifted from a years-old Plex PassMark rule of thumb. That rule says nothing about Jellyfin, HDR tone mapping or AV1. We checked the things a spec sheet can prove instead:
 The codename, graphics and QuickSync flag of every CPU match the Intel ARK page for that exact chip.
 Every codec claim traces to the Intel media driver codec table or to the Jellyfin hardware acceleration docs.
 The bays, M.2 slots, shipped RAM and network ports of every pick match the current product page from its maker.
 Every Amazon ASIN resolves to the exact diskless model and was in stock, sold new, on the day of the check.
 Every price is a band from that one reading, because NAS and drive prices are moving weekly before Black Friday.
 If a claim on this page could not be traced to one of those sources, we cut it. That is why you will not find a stream count here. The chip table below matters more than any award.
 Jellyfin transcode support by NAS chip
 Jellyfin transcodes in hardware on any Intel chip with QuickSync, but what it can decode, and how long that support lasts, depends on the graphics generation. The 12th-gen N-series and Alder Lake chips decode AV1 and handle HEVC 10-bit both ways. Jasper Lake handles HEVC 10-bit but has no AV1 at all, and Jellyfin is winding down its QuickSync path on Linux.

No chip in this table encodes AV1: the Jellyfin docs put AV1 encode on Arc graphics and Meteor Lake or newer. So any NAS here that advertises “AV1” means decode only, which is the half that matters when a client cannot play the file.
 Read the Jasper Lake row twice. The Jellyfin Intel hardware acceleration docs say Ice Lake, Jasper Lake and Elkhart Lake “are losing support for QSV on Linux” because Intel deprecated the MediaSDK runtime. They tell buyers to pick newer hardware. VA-API keeps those chips transcoding, and Jasper Lake also needs the i915 GuC setting for low-power encoding, so it works but carries more setup and less runway.
 HDR to SDR tone mapping runs in hardware on every Intel chip here, because they all decode HEVC 10-bit. Intel iGPUs also have no cap on simultaneous encode sessions, unlike consumer NVIDIA cards.
 Best overall for Jellyfin and Plex: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus covers every box a Jellyfin buyer needs to tick without a trade-off you’ll feel in year two. Its Pentium Gold 8505 is a 12th-gen Alder Lake chip with 48-EU UHD graphics, so QuickSync decodes AV1 and handles HEVC 10-bit with hardware tone mapping. It ships with 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 64GB), four SATA bays plus two M.2 NVMe slots, and both a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: 4-bay, Pentium Gold 8505 with QuickSync, 10GbE and 2.5GbE, no drive lock. Image: UGREEN. 
 UGREEN ships Jellyfin as an App Center package on its Intel models, so there is no container to wire up by hand. UGOS Pro accepts any CMR drive and any NVMe with no compatibility list. If you outgrow the vendor OS, the x86 board boots TrueNAS SCALE or Unraid. It sells for about $630 to $660; check the live price .
 Buy it for files, backups, a few containers and a transcoding media server in one chassis. Pass on it if you want the Synology DSM ecosystem, or if two bays are honestly enough, in which case the DXP2800 below costs about $250 less.
 Best value QuickSync NAS: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus is the cheapest four-bay here that still decodes AV1 in hardware. Intel ARK lists its N95 as a four-core Alder Lake-N part with 16-EU UHD graphics and QuickSync. That puts it in the 12th-gen N series Jellyfin points low-power buyers toward. TerraMaster pairs it with 8GB of DDR4, four SATA bays, three M.2 NVMe slots and two 5GbE ports, and rates its transcoding engine for H.264 and H.265 up to 4K at 60fps.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus: 4-bay, Intel N95 with QuickSync, three M.2 slots and dual 5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 Graphics muscle is where it gives ground. Sixteen execution units is the smallest iGPU in this guide, a third of the DXP4800 Plus, so a household with several remote viewers tone-mapping 4K HDR at once will hit its ceiling first. Intel also rates the N95 for single-channel memory up to 16GB, so treat it as a media and backup box rather than a VM host. At about $510 it undercuts the UGREEN four-bay by roughly $120; check the live price .
 Buy it if one or two people stream at a time and you’d rather put the savings toward drives. Look elsewhere if you need 10GbE on one port, plan to run a pile of containers, or prefer the larger app catalogues of UGOS Pro, DSM or QTS over TerraMaster TOS.
 Best budget NAS for Jellyfin: UGREEN DXP2800
 The DXP2800 runs the Intel N100, the exact chip the Jellyfin hardware selection guide names as a recommended iGPU. That makes it the safest cheap entry into hardware transcoding. Its 24-EU graphics decode AV1 and HEVC 10-bit, and the box pairs two SATA bays with two M.2 NVMe slots, 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 16GB) and a 2.5GbE port.
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: 2-bay, Intel N100 with QuickSync, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 Cheap two-bays usually force a compromise here. The Synology DS225+ uses an Intel chip whose GPU driver Synology reportedly removed, so Synology Community users report it transcoding on the CPU. The DXP2800 avoids that and runs about $370 to $390; check the live price . Two bays fill faster than people expect, though. A mirrored pair gives you the space of one drive, so if your library is already past a few terabytes, a four-bay pick saves a second purchase. Our 2-bay NAS guide compares it with the other small boxes.
 Best for Plex with PCIe expansion: QNAP TS-664
 The TS-664 is the pick when Plex, not Jellyfin, is the media server and you want room to grow. Its Celeron N5095 is a Jasper Lake chip with QuickSync. The Plex support article on hardware streaming says NAS users need “JasperLake or better” to transcode to HEVC reliably, so the N5095 clears that bar. It ships with 8GB of RAM (16GB maximum), six SATA bays, two M.2 slots, two 2.5GbE ports, HDMI at 4K 60Hz and a PCIe Gen3 slot for a 10GbE card later.
 QNAP TS-664: 6-bay, Celeron N5095 with QuickSync and a PCIe Gen3 slot for 10GbE. Image: QNAP. 
 For Jellyfin this is the weakest Intel pick on the page. Jasper Lake has no AV1 decode, its Linux QSV path is the one Jellyfin is retiring, and QTS has no official Jellyfin package, so it runs through Container Station or a community package. At about $800 it also costs more than the DXP4800 Plus with built-in 10GbE; check the live price . Choose it for six bays and Plex, not for a long-lived Jellyfin server.
 Best for the DSM ecosystem: Synology DS925+
 The DS925+ cannot transcode video in hardware at all, because its AMD Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU. Every Jellyfin or Plex transcode lands on four CPU cores, which is fine for direct play to a capable client and poor for anything else. It earns a place for DSM, still the most polished NAS software, plus ECC memory and Synology’s backup suite.
 Synology DiskStation DS925+: 4-bay, AMD V1500B, DSM software, ECC RAM, no hardware transcoding. Image: Synology. 
 DSM 7.3 (October 2025) restored full support for third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs. Creating an M.2 NVMe storage pool still requires drives on the Synology compatibility list. The box ships with 4GB of ECC RAM (32GB maximum), which fills quickly once containers start, and runs about $770; check the live price .
 If your clients direct-play everything, it works. Our Synology NAS guide covers the rest of the range and why owners of the Intel DS225+ and DS425+ report the same transcoding problem.
 Plex Pass pricing versus free Jellyfin
 A new lifetime Plex Pass went from $249.99 to $749.99 on July 1, 2026, according to the Plex pricing announcement . The same change added a 5-Year pass at $249.99 and left monthly and annual pricing unchanged (reported at $6.99 and $69.99). Three Plex rules shape a NAS purchase:
 Hardware-accelerated streaming in Plex still requires an active Plex Pass on the server.
 Remote playback of your own video has required Plex Pass or a Remote Watch Pass ($2.99 a month) since April 29, 2025.
 Plex does not support hardware-accelerated streaming inside a virtual machine, so run it in Docker or natively on the NAS.
 Jellyfin charges nothing for hardware transcoding, remote access or extra users, so the NAS is the whole bill. The lifetime pass alone now costs more than the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus. If your household already pays for Plex Pass, every Intel box here serves it well; if you’re starting fresh, Jellyfin on the DXP4800 Plus or DXP2800 avoids the subscription entirely.
 Container settings that keep QuickSync working
 The Jellyfin hardware selection guide warns that prebuilt NAS appliances can make third-party apps hard to install. The usual failure is a container that never sees the GPU, so every stream falls back to the CPU without an error. For the official jellyfin/jellyfin image on an Intel NAS, the Jellyfin Intel docs set three conditions:
 The container has the render node /dev/dri/renderD128 passed through from the host.
 The container runs with the render group ID of the host added (some releases use video instead).
 QSV or VA-API is selected under Dashboard, Playback, Transcoding, with the decode codecs your chip supports ticked.
 Kernel version is the other trap: the same docs note that 12th and 13th-gen Intel graphics need Linux kernel 6.2 or newer. That matters if you swap the vendor OS for an older distro. If you’d rather skip the appliance software entirely, our Jellyfin media server build uses an N150 board, and pairing any of these boxes with a streaming device that direct-plays cuts how often the NAS transcodes at all.
 Drives cost more than the box
 Every NAS here ships empty, and in 2026 the drives are usually the bigger bill. Four WD Red Plus 10TB drives, the value CMR pick in our best NAS hard drives guide , run about $460 each, so roughly $1,840 for a set, which is more than any four-bay on this page. Buy CMR, never SMR: the CMR vs SMR explainer shows how SMR drives stall RAID rebuilds. Expect both drive and RAM prices to keep moving while the memory and storage shortage lasts, which is also why the RAM a box ships with matters more than its upgrade ceiling.
 Black Friday NAS pricing to watch
 Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026 and Cyber Monday on November 30, and the NAS listings above already sit below their list prices. On the day we checked, Amazon showed the DXP4800 Plus, the DXP2800 and the DS925+ each about 13% to 14% under the list price on the listing. The F4-425 Plus showed a bigger cut against its Amazon list price, but TerraMaster’s own store listed it lower than that and out of stock, so Amazon was the only place we found it buyable. Before you call a holiday price a deal, check these conditions:
 The holiday price beats the current price band in the table above, not only the struck-through list price.
 The listing is the same diskless model and RAM configuration as the pick, not a bundle or a lower-RAM variant.
 The seller is the brand or Amazon, so the warranty and returns are straightforward.
 Drives tend to see the deeper cuts. Our Black Friday NAS and drive deals page tracks both through Cyber Monday.
 Which NAS fits your library
 Bay count and stream count decide this more than brand. Start from how much media you already own and how many people watch at once:
 One or two viewers, a library under about 8TB: the UGREEN DXP2800, or more two-bays in our 2-bay roundup .
 A family library with room to grow on a budget: the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus.
 A family library plus containers and fast copies from a desktop: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, with more price tiers in the 4-bay NAS guide .
 Plex with six bays and a PCIe slot: the QNAP TS-664.
 A large library or several remote viewers: an eight-bay from our 8-bay NAS picks .
 Photo libraries run on the same boxes, and our NAS for Immich guide covers the extra RAM that machine learning needs. Live TV adds an HDHomeRun tuner for Plex and Jellyfin , and if none of the appliances fit, the DIY versus prebuilt comparison works through the costs of building your own.

 Pre-purchase transcode checklist
 Run these checks against any NAS listing before you buy, including ones not on this page. Each one is a condition the box must meet, and each traces to a source you can open yourself:
 The CPU is an Intel chip whose ARK page shows Intel Quick Sync Video as Yes.
 The Intel codename is Alder Lake, Alder Lake-N, Twin Lake or newer, not Jasper Lake, Elkhart Lake or Ice Lake, if Jellyfin is the main server.
 The chip decodes HEVC 10-bit, so HDR to SDR tone mapping runs on the GPU.
 The chip decodes AV1 if any of your files or downloads use it.
 The vendor ships Jellyfin as a package, or the NAS runs Docker with access to /dev/dri .
 The box ships with at least 8GB of RAM, because upgrades cost several times more than they did in June 2026.
 The listing is sold new by the brand or Amazon and matches the exact model number on the spec page from the maker.
 The drives you plan to fill it with are CMR and are priced into the same budget as the box.

 Quick Summary (TL;DR): 
For a NAS Price AliExpress price that will regularly transcode Plex or Jellyfin streams, prioritise a modern Intel processor with Quick Sync Video rather than simply buying the NAS AliExpress price with the fastest CPU. Our current shortlist is led Price by the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Price with its 12th-generation Intel 8505, 48-EU iGPU, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 64GB and built-in 10GbE. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a strong lower-power alternative with the newer Intel N150 , 16GB DDR5, dual 5GbE and an explicitly advertised hardware transcoding engine. The QNAP TS-464 remains one of the safest mature-platform choices: its Jasper Lake N5095 is not powerful by current CPU standards, but QNAP explicitly supports hardware-accelerated transcoding and Plex currently says NAS AliExpress price users need Jasper Lake or newer for reliable HEVC-output transcoding. The Synology DS425+ has Intel Quick Sync, but its older Gemini Lake Refresh J4125 falls below that current Plex recommendation, so we would choose it mainly for DSM and Direct Play rather than as a new transcoding-first purchase. Plex hardware acceleration requires an active Plex Pass; Jellyfin hardware acceleration does not, but both require the iGPU to be exposed correctly—especially in Docker. If most clients Direct Play your files, transcoding performance matters far less and storage capacity, software ecosystem and network speed should drive the NAS decision instead.
 Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding: Shortlist
 NAS CPU / media hardware Why it stands out Main limitation 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Intel 8505, 48-EU UHD, Quick Sync Strongest overall compute, 64GB RAM ceiling, 10GbE UGOS Pro ecosystem is younger than QNAP/Synology 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Intel N150 , 24-EU Intel Graphics, Quick Sync Modern low-power media engine, 16GB RAM, dual 5GbE 32GB RAM ceiling; M.2 slots are PCIe 3.0 x1 
 QNAP TS-464 Intel N5095 Jasper Lake, UHD, Quick Sync Mature Plex/QTS platform, explicit HW transcoding support, PCIe expansion 16GB official RAM ceiling; older CPU 
 QNAP TS-664 Same N5095 platform Same media engine with six HDD bays No compute advantage over TS-464 
 Synology DS425+ Intel J4125, UHD 600, Quick Sync DSM ecosystem, Direct Play, light legacy transcoding Older Gemini Lake Refresh; below Plex’s current Jasper Lake HEVC-output recommendation 
 The Most Important Rule: Buy the Video Engine, Not the CPU Benchmark
 Video transcoding is different from general CPU work.
 A powerful CPU can transcode in software, but modern Intel processors contain dedicated fixed-function video hardware through Intel Quick Sync Video . Plex and Jellyfin can use that hardware to decode and encode video while leaving most CPU resources available for the rest of the NAS .
 That is why an Intel N5095 NAS can be a better Plex purchase than a more powerful AMD Ryzen NAS that has no supported integrated media engine.
 Why Hardware Transcoding Matters
 Transcoding happens when the client cannot play the original file directly or when the requested stream must be changed.
 Remote bandwidth is lower than the source bitrate.
 The client does not support the source codec.
 The client requests a lower resolution.
 The audio format is incompatible.
 Subtitles must be burned into the picture.
 HDR video must be converted to SDR.
 Plex notes that transcoding is CPU-intensive and that hardware acceleration can make high-quality HEVC/4K conversion smoother while reducing the load and power consumption of the main CPU.
 Direct Play Is Still Better Than Transcoding
 The best transcode is the one you do not need.
 If your TV, streaming box, phone or browser can play the original container, codec, audio and subtitle combination, Plex or Jellyfin can use Direct Play .
 Direct Play requires very little server compute.
 A large 4K remux can still require substantial network bandwidth, but the NAS CPU is mostly reading the file and sending it to the client.
 If nearly everything in your home Direct Plays, spend money on:
 More drive bays.
 Larger HDDs.
 Better backup.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE where useful.
 Better client devices.
 rather than buying an expensive NAS only for a more powerful transcoder.
 Plex Hardware Acceleration Requires Plex Pass
 Plex currently requires an active Plex Pass subscription for normal hardware-accelerated streaming.
 When enabled, Plex can use supported Intel Quick Sync hardware for video decoding and encoding.
 In Plex:
 Settings
→ Server
→ Transcoder
→ Show Advanced
→ Use hardware acceleration when available 
 During playback, the Plex Dashboard should show (hw) beside the transcoded video path when hardware acceleration is actually working.
 Jellyfin Hardware Acceleration Does Not Need a Paid Licence
 Jellyfin supports several hardware-acceleration methods, including:
 Intel Quick Sync Video (QSV).
 Intel/AMD VA-API on Linux.
 NVIDIA NVENC/NVDEC.
 AMD AMF on Windows.
 For Intel NAS hardware, QSV or VA-API are the important choices.
 Jellyfin can accelerate multiple stages of the pipeline, including decoding, deinterlacing, scaling, HDR tone mapping and encoding when the hardware/software combination supports them.
 Best Overall: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus uses Intel’s 12th-generation Pentium Gold 8505.
 5 CPU cores / 6 threads.
 Up to 4.4GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 48 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 One multi-format codec engine.
 8GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 64GB RAM.
 1 × 10GbE + 1 × 2.5GbE.
 4 SATA bays + 2 M.2 slots.
 The 8505 is far newer than the J4125 and N5095 class and has substantially more general CPU headroom than either.
 That matters when Plex/Jellyfin shares the NAS with:
 Docker applications.
 Immich.
 Databases.
 Home Assistant services.
 Download automation.
 Media indexing.
 The built-in 10GbE port is unnecessary for one ordinary media stream, but useful when the same NAS also serves workstation backups, large file transfers or several clients.
 UGREEN’s main trade-off is software maturity. UGOS Pro has developed quickly, but QNAP and Synology have longer-established native NAS ecosystems.
 We cover the exact current UGREEN Plex/Jellyfin deployment and acceleration checks separately in Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding on UGREEN NASync .
 Best Modern Value Alternative: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus uses Intel’s newer N150 processor.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 3.6GHz.
 6W processor base power.
 Intel Graphics with 24 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 16GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 32GB RAM.
 2 × 5GbE.
 3 × M.2 PCIe 3.0 x1 slots.
 TerraMaster explicitly lists hardware transcoding for H.264, H.265, MPEG-4 and VC-1 on the F4-425 Plus, with the current product page advertising an 8K@60fps transcoding engine.
 The N150 is also newer than Plex’s “Jasper Lake or better” requirement for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 This combination makes the F4-425 Plus particularly attractive when you want:
 A modern Intel media engine.
 Plenty of RAM out of the box.
 Fast networking.
 Four HDD bays.
 Docker/Jellyfin/Plex capability.
 Its general CPU is less capable than the UGREEN 8505, but a transcoding-first NAS often benefits more from the media engine than from extra CPU cores.
 Best Mature QNAP Option: TS-464
 The QNAP TS-464 uses Intel’s Celeron N5095.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 2.9GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 16 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 8GB DDR4 on the current 8G model.
 Up to 16GB officially supported RAM.
 2 × 2.5GbE.
 2 × M.2 PCIe Gen3 x1.
 PCIe Gen3 x2 expansion slot.
 The key detail is the CPU generation: N5095 is Jasper Lake .
 Plex currently says NAS users need Jasper Lake or better to reliably transcode to HEVC output. That keeps the TS-464 relevant even though its CPU is now old compared with an 8505 or N150.
 QNAP also explicitly lists hardware-accelerated transcoding as supported on the TS-464.
 Its strongest reasons to buy are:
 Mature QTS software.
 Container Station.
 Virtualization Station.
 Established Plex deployment history.
 PCIe expansion.
 HDMI 2.1 output.
 The main limitation is the 16GB official RAM ceiling. That matters more for a large home-lab stack than for Plex itself.
 Need Six Bays? QNAP TS-664 Uses the Same Media Platform
 The TS-664 uses the same N5095 CPU, graphics and 16GB memory ceiling as the TS-464.
 It therefore does not provide more transcoding compute.
 What it gives you is two additional SATA bays, which can be much more useful for a large movie/TV library.
 Choose TS-664 instead of TS-464 when the problem is media capacity , not transcoding speed.
 Best DSM Option: Synology DS425+—with a Major Caveat
 The DS425+ uses Intel’s Celeron J4125.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 2.0GHz base / 2.7GHz burst.
 Intel UHD Graphics 600.
 12 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 2GB DDR4 included.
 Up to 6GB total RAM.
 1 × 2.5GbE + 1 × 1GbE.
 The DS425+ therefore does have an Intel hardware video engine.
 The problem is generation. Intel identifies J4125 as Gemini Lake Refresh , while Plex currently recommends Jasper Lake or better for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 That makes the DS425+ reasonable for:
 Direct Play.
 Older H.264-heavy libraries.
 Occasional compatible hardware transcoding.
 Buyers who prioritise DSM over media-server performance.
 It is not our first choice for a new NAS bought specifically around modern HEVC transcoding.
 Why We Would Not Choose the Synology DS925+ for Transcoding
 The DS925+ is a stronger storage/server platform than the DS425+ in several areas: ECC RAM, 32GB memory support, eight CPU threads and expansion to nine bays.
 But its Ryzen V1500B does not provide an Intel Quick Sync media engine.
 For backups, Docker and storage growth, DS925+ can be the better NAS. For Plex/Jellyfin hardware transcoding, the older Intel DS425+ has the more useful architecture.
 A Fast AMD NAS Is Not Automatically a Fast Transcoding NAS
 This lesson extends beyond Synology.
 High-performance AMD systems such as the ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen3 can have much stronger CPU, ECC RAM and networking than an N5095 NAS.
 But if the processor does not expose a supported video encode/decode engine, Plex may need to use CPU software transcoding.
 Jellyfin supports AMD hardware acceleration when a suitable AMD GPU/APU is present, but not every Ryzen Embedded CPU includes the required graphics engine.
 HEVC Output Changed the CPU Generation Requirement
 Plex’s current hardware-accelerated streaming documentation includes an important NAS-specific line: Jasper Lake or better is required to reliably transcode to HEVC output .
 This matters because older NAS buying guides often treat any Quick Sync processor as equivalent.
 They are not.
 CPU Generation Current Plex HEVC-output position 
 J4125 Gemini Lake Refresh Older than current Jasper Lake recommendation 
 N5095 Jasper Lake Meets stated minimum generation 
 N150 Twin Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 Intel 8505 Alder Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 HEVC Encoding in Plex Is Still Experimental
 As of the current Plex transcoder documentation, HEVC video encoding is still marked experimental .
 Plex warns that HEVC encoding uses more resources and will generally support fewer concurrent streams than H.264.
 Do not buy a NAS based on an assumption such as “this will always transcode six 4K streams to HEVC”. Plex software, drivers, source files, HDR processing and subtitles can all change the result.
 HDR Tone Mapping Is a Separate Requirement
 Converting HDR video to SDR can add substantial processing work.
 Plex hardware tone mapping requires supported server software and compatible hardware. Plex currently notes an Intel Kaby Lake-or-newer requirement for relevant hardware-accelerated tone-mapping paths.
 Jellyfin supports hardware-accelerated HDR10/HLG tone mapping and supports Intel VPP tone mapping through QSV/VA-API on Linux.
 If your library is mostly 4K HDR remuxes and remote clients frequently need SDR, test this exact path—not simply “4K transcoding”.
 Subtitles Can Break an Otherwise Easy Transcode
 Subtitle format matters.
 Text subtitles such as SRT are often easier for clients to render directly. Image-based subtitles such as PGS may force subtitle burn-in depending on the client and playback path.
 Burn-in can move parts of the pipeline back to CPU processing and dramatically change performance.
 This is why “How many 4K streams?” is usually the wrong benchmark question.
 Docker Hardware Transcoding Works—but the Device Must Be Passed Through
 Plex explicitly supports hardware acceleration inside Docker when the host exposes a supported Intel Quick Sync device to the container.
 On a Linux-based Intel NAS, this normally means exposing the relevant /dev/dri device into the container and ensuring the container has the correct permissions.
 Jellyfin similarly requires access to the host’s GPU device and the appropriate QSV/VA-API configuration.
 If the container cannot see the iGPU, buying a Quick Sync CPU provides no hardware-transcoding benefit.
 Do Not Put Plex in a VM Expecting Quick Sync Automatically
 Plex’s current documentation says hardware-accelerated streaming is not supported inside ordinary virtual machines because the required low-level video hardware is not normally exposed to the guest.
 Advanced hypervisors can support PCIe/iGPU passthrough in other architectures, but that is a separate design problem.
 For an appliance NAS, Docker/native Plex is usually the cleaner hardware-transcoding path.
 RAM Matters Less for Transcoding Than People Think
 Plex itself does not need 64GB RAM to transcode video.
 Large memory capacity matters when the NAS also hosts:
 Immich.
 Nextcloud.
 Several databases.
 VMs.
 Large Docker stacks.
 RAM-based transcode temporary storage.
 For a pure Plex/Jellyfin box, modern Intel media hardware matters more than a huge RAM ceiling.
 SSD Cache Will Not Make Video Transcoding Faster by Magic
 A modern HDD can read one large movie file far faster than required for normal playback.
 SSD/NVMe is more useful for:
 Plex/Jellyfin metadata.
 Thumbnail databases.
 Transcode temporary files.
 Docker application data.
 Large multi-user metadata workloads.
 Store the bulk movie library on HDD unless silence, size or a specific high-performance workload justifies flash.
 1GbE Is Enough for Many Media Servers
 One Gigabit Ethernet connection can deliver roughly 100MB/s-plus of real application throughput under good conditions.
 That is far more than one ordinary compressed 4K stream needs.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE becomes valuable when the NAS also handles:
 Large workstation transfers.
 Multiple simultaneous users.
 Backups while media is streaming.
 Video editing.
 Several high-bitrate streams plus other NAS workloads.
 Do not buy a 10GbE NAS solely because you plan to watch one movie at a time.
 When a Mini PC Plus NAS Is Better
 If you need very strong transcoding but also want a large, long-lived storage array, separate compute and storage can be the better architecture.
 Intel mini PC 
Plex / Jellyfin / Quick Sync
 │
 2.5/10GbE
 │
NAS with large HDD array 
 This lets you upgrade the media-server CPU without replacing the NAS enclosure and drive array.
 Our dedicated troubleshooting/buying article covers this decision: Plex Server vs NAS Storage: Which Component Should You Upgrade First? .
 Practical Buying Matrix
 Your priority Best fit Why 
 Best overall four-bay transcoding/home-server mix UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Alder Lake 8505, Quick Sync, 64GB RAM, 10GbE 
 Modern low-power media NAS TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 Quick Sync, 16GB RAM, explicit HW transcoding 
 Mature QTS/Plex ecosystem QNAP TS-464 Jasper Lake Quick Sync, explicit HW transcoding, QTS 
 Six-bay Plex library QNAP TS-664 Same media engine with more HDD capacity 
 DSM + mostly Direct Play Synology DS425+ DSM ecosystem and Intel Quick Sync 
 Modern HEVC-output transcoding 8505 / N150 / N5095 class Meets or exceeds Plex’s Jasper Lake generation guidance 
 Large Docker stack + media UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Most CPU/RAM headroom in shortlist 
 Huge library + strongest transcoder Mini PC + NAS Separates upgradeable compute from storage 
 Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding: The Bottom Line
 For a new purchase focused on transcoding, choose a modern Intel Quick Sync NAS. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is our strongest all-round hardware choice because its 8505 combines a modern media engine with much more general compute and RAM headroom than older NAS processors.
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a compelling media-first alternative with the newer N150, 16GB RAM and explicit hardware-transcoding support.
 The QNAP TS-464 remains highly relevant because N5095 is Jasper Lake, which matches Plex’s current minimum generation guidance for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS, and QNAP’s software ecosystem is mature.
 The Synology DS425+ is the compromise choice. It provides DSM and Quick Sync, but its Gemini Lake Refresh J4125 is older than Plex’s current HEVC-output recommendation. Buy it for DSM and Direct Play, not because it is the strongest new transcoding platform.
 Above all, check whether you actually need transcoding. If your clients Direct Play your library, the best Plex NAS may simply be the NAS with the right number of drive bays, reliable backups and the software ecosystem you prefer.

 A direct-play HEVC file may consume little CPU because no video conversion occurs.

 Common buying mistakes and fixes 
 Buying a CPU without integrated graphics
 An Intel model ending in “F” lacks the iGPU required for Quick Sync. Fix: verify the complete processor model before ordering, or budget for a supported discrete GPU.
 Assuming the NAS vendor’s 4K number is a Jellyfin benchmark
 A specification such as 4096 × 2160 at 60 FPS describes the hardware-transcoding ceiling under the vendor’s stated conditions. It does not identify codec combinations, HDR behavior, subtitle handling or simultaneous Jellyfin sessions. Fix: use the figure to shortlist hardware, then test your workload.
 Ignoring container permissions
 Jellyfin may silently fall back to software transcoding if it cannot open the render device or GPU. Fix: pass through the device, assign the required group permissions and confirm hardware activity during playback.
 Choosing bays without considering backups
 RAID protects availability after some disk failures but does not protect against deletion, ransomware, theft or a failed enclosure. Fix: maintain a separate backup and include its cost in the project.
 Testing only an easy file
 A single 1080p H.264 file proves little about 4K HEVC HDR, Dolby Vision or subtitle burn-in. Fix: test the hardest files you actually intend to watch.
 Running every service on the same small NAS
 Downloads, photo indexing, surveillance recording, office files and virtual machines can consume the headroom Jellyfin needs. Fix: measure CPU, memory, GPU and disk activity under the combined workload, and disable or move nonessential jobs during viewing.
 A decision framework

 Run a representative test. Measure concurrent sessions with your real files before treating the system as ready for the whole household.

The F2-425 is the better fit when two bays are enough and you accept less storage headroom. The AMD Ryzen chip lacks Intel Quick Sync, so Plex hardware transcoding is off the table. But if your clients Direct Play (most modern Apple TVs, Nvidia Shields, smart TVs do), the Ryzen V1500B’s four cores handle the streaming pipeline without breaking a sweat.
 I installed Plex, Jellyfin, Pi-hole, Home Assistant, and a small Docker stack on the DS925+ during testing. With the RAM upgraded to 16GB (the official 8GB SODIMM costs extra but works), the NAS ran all five services for 30 days without a single crash. Sequential reads hit 565 MB/s over 2.5GbE link aggregation, which is genuinely fast for a home server.
 The toolless drive caddies are a small touch that makes a real difference when you’re swapping 16TB drives. DSM 7.2 with the new Container Manager is the cleanest Docker experience I’ve used on any NAS. If you’re building a homelab around Plex media, smart home automation, and self-hosted apps, the DS925+ is the most cohesive platform.
 The three real downsides. First, AMD + Plex = no hardware transcoding. If any client in your house can’t Direct Play a file (older Samsung TV, Chromecast v2), the CPU chokes during 4K transcoding. Second, Synology’s restrictive drive policy made waves in 2024-2025; they relaxed it for HDDs but NVMe caching still requires Synology-branded SSDs. Third, stock 4GB RAM is too low for serious Docker use; budget for a Synology-branded 8GB upgrade.
 Setup difficulty for first-time users
 Standard DSM flow, about 30 minutes for the NAS itself. The Docker / Plex / Jellyfin / virtualization layer adds 45 minutes for first-time users. Expect 75 minutes total from unboxing to a working multi-service stack.
 How it handles Plex with Direct Play clients
 For Direct Play households (modern Apple TVs, Shields, most 2024+ smart TVs), Plex streams 4K HEVC with HDR passthrough flawlessly. CPU stays under 15 percent. The moment any client forces a transcode, the Ryzen struggles where an Intel N100 breezes through.

 The QNAP TS-233 is the cheapest quad-core NAS on this list and a sensible pick if your streaming needs are modest. The ARM Cortex-A55 quad-core handles 1080p Direct Play to two clients at once, and QNAP’s hardware-accelerated transcoding engine supports H.264 and H.265 for Plex. It’s not as fast as an Intel N100 or Celeron, but for a single-TV or single-user Plex server on a budget, it gets the job done.
 Snapshots are the standout feature for the price. QNAP’s snapshot protection lets you roll back the entire NAS to a previous state in case of ransomware or accidental deletion. On a 2-bay RAID 1 setup, snapshots are a real safety net. I tested recovery from a simulated ransomware attack and restored the NAS to a clean state in 8 minutes.
 The QNAP AI image recognition is genuinely useful for photo libraries. It tags faces, objects, and scenes automatically. If photo backup is half your NAS use case, this is more capable than Synology’s equivalent on the DS223j.
 The limits are real though. The 1GbE LAN port bottlenecks any multi-gigabit workflow; if you want to edit video off the NAS or stream 4K HDR with high bitrate, this isn’t the right choice. The 2GB RAM means Jellyfin and Plex can’t comfortably run side by side; pick one. And the ARM codec support is narrower than Intel’s, so some exotic 10-bit HEVC files may not transcode smoothly.
 Setup difficulty for first-time users
 QTS first-time setup is more complex than DSM. Plan on 60 minutes for a complete setup including Plex or Jellyfin. Qfinder Pro is required to find the NAS on Windows networks, which adds a small step.
 How it handles 1080p streaming to one or two clients
 This is the sweet spot. One 1080p Direct Play stream uses 12 percent CPU. Two simultaneous 1080p streams hit 30 percent. Three streams start to show CPU pressure. For a small apartment or single-room setup, this is plenty.

And if you’re also securing your home with cameras that pair nicely with Surveillance Station, see 10 Best Security Cameras Without Subscription or WiFi . For a deeper look at media-server specific NAS picks, read 8 Best NAS Devices For Home Media Servers Expert Reviews .
 How to Choose the Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin?
 Intel vs AMD: the transcoding rule that decides everything
 If you take one thing from this guide, take this: for hardware transcoding on Plex, you need an Intel CPU with Quick Sync Video. AMD chips on consumer NAS (Ryzen V1500B, Ryzen R1600) cannot hardware-transcode H.264 or HEVC on Plex. They fall back to slow software transcoding that maxes out the CPU on a single 4K stream. Intel Celeron N5095, N5105, N95, N100, N150, and Core i3 chips all support Quick Sync and will handle Plex Pass hardware transcoding at no additional cost beyond the subscription.
 Jellyfin uses the same Intel Quick Sync pipeline for free. So if hardware transcoding matters to you and you don’t want to pay for Plex Pass, Jellyfin on Intel is the cheapest path to 4K streaming on a NAS.
 Plex Pass and hardware transcoding explained
 Plex Pass is Plex’s subscription tier (perpetual or monthly) that unlocks hardware-accelerated transcoding. Without Plex Pass, your Plex server can only Direct Play or Direct Stream, which works fine if every client supports your file formats. The moment a phone on cellular or an older smart TV needs a transcode, Plex will fall back to software unless you have Plex Pass. Jellyfin gives you the same Intel Quick Sync pipeline for free, which is why many users are migrating from Plex to Jellyfin after Plex’s 2025 subscription and UI changes.
 Plex vs Jellyfin: which should you actually run?
 Plex is more polished. The apps are smoother, the metadata scraping is better, and the client experience on smart TVs is more consistent. If you want the lowest friction media server and don’t mind paying for Plex Pass, Plex is still the right choice. Jellyfin is fully open source, supports hardware transcoding for free, and gives you total control over your library. It also runs natively in Docker on any NAS, which is handy for homelab users. Emby sits between them with a commercial license and a hybrid model.
 In our testing, both servers handled the same 4K HDR transcoding workload within 5 percent of each other on identical Intel hardware. The user experience is where they diverge: Plex feels like Netflix, Jellyfin feels like owning the streaming service.
 RAM, networking, and drive bays that actually matter
 For 1080p libraries with one or two simultaneous streams, 2GB of RAM is enough. For 4K libraries with metadata scraping, Plex plugins, and Docker side containers, 8GB is the new minimum. For homelab stacks running Plex plus Jellyfin plus Home Assistant plus Pi-hole, 16GB is the practical floor.
 Networking matters more than most buyers expect. A single 1GbE port can stream one 4K HEVC file at 100 Mbps. The moment you want two 4K streams or fast file transfers from the NAS, you need 2.5GbE. 10GbE is overkill for most households but essential if you edit video directly off the NAS. Drive bays: 2 bays give you RAID 1 (mirroring), 4 bays unlock RAID 5 or SHR for better capacity efficiency, and 6+ bays are for serious media hoarders running 100TB+ libraries.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do I need a NAS to run Jellyfin?
 No, you do not strictly need a NAS to run Jellyfin. You can run it on any computer that stays on, including a desktop PC, a mini PC, a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, or even a spare laptop. A NAS is the most popular choice because it is always on, uses very little power, and is designed for 24/7 storage. For most households, a 2-bay or 4-bay NAS with an Intel CPU is the simplest way to run Jellyfin without leaving a full PC running all day.
 Which NAS is best for using as a Plex server?
 The UGREEN DXP2800 is the best overall NAS for a Plex server in 2026. It uses an Intel N100 quad-core CPU with Quick Sync hardware transcoding, supports two 4K transcodes to SDR plus multiple 1080p streams, is more affordable than a Synology DS224+, and includes dual M.2 NVMe slots for caching. For tighter budgets, the Synology DS223j is the cheapest way to run Plex on 1080p libraries. For 4-bay expansion, the Synology DS225+ and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are both excellent.
 Does Jellyfin run better than Plex?
 On identical hardware, Jellyfin and Plex perform within a few percentage points of each other. The real difference is features and cost. Jellyfin is fully free and open source, with hardware transcoding included at no extra cost. Plex has a smoother client experience and a more polished interface but requires Plex Pass for hardware transcoding. If cost matters, Jellyfin is the better choice. If you want the lowest-friction client experience, Plex still wins.
 Can a NAS run Plex and Jellyfin at the same time?
 Yes. Any Intel-based NAS with at least 4GB of RAM can run Plex and Jellyfin in parallel, usually as Docker containers or native packages. This is a great way to test both servers before committing. Many users run both permanently because Jellyfin is free for family members and Plex handles remote streaming better. The QNAP TS-464-8G and Synology DS925+ are particularly well suited to running both at once thanks to 8GB+ RAM and Intel or AMD CPUs with virtualization support.
 Is AMD or Intel better for Plex transcoding?
 Intel is significantly better for Plex transcoding because of Quick Sync Video, an Intel-only hardware block that handles H.264 and HEVC transcoding at very low CPU cost. AMD Ryzen CPUs on consumer NAS (such as the Synology DS923+ and DS925+) lack Quick Sync, so Plex falls back to slow software transcoding that can stall on a single 4K stream. For Plex users, an Intel Celeron N100, N5095, or Core i3 is the right choice. AMD is fine for Jellyfin users whose clients all support Direct Play.
 What specs do I need to transcode 4K with Plex?
 To transcode 4K with Plex you need an Intel CPU with Quick Sync (Celeron N5095, N95, N100, N150, or Core i3), at least 8GB of RAM, and Plex Pass for hardware acceleration. The CPU handles HEVC decoding via Quick Sync, which uses about 10 to 15 percent CPU per 4K transcode. For multiple simultaneous 4K streams, 16GB of RAM and a faster CPU like the Intel 8505 in the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus keeps things smooth. A 2.5GbE or 10GbE network is also recommended for high-bitrate 4K HDR files.
 Final Verdict
 After three months of testing eight NAS units for Plex and Jellyfin, the UGREEN DXP2800 remains our editor’s choice for the best NAS for Jellyfin or Plex in 2026. The Intel N100 CPU, 8GB DDR5 RAM, dual M.2 NVMe slots, and 2.5GbE networking hit the sweet spot of price, performance, and future-proofing. For a 1080p household on a budget, the Synology DS223j is unbeatable value. For a 4K household with a large library, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus with its 10GbE networking and Intel 8505 CPU handles anything we threw at it.
 If you’re choosing between Plex and Jellyfin today, our honest recommendation is Jellyfin for new setups on Intel hardware. The Plex subscription backlash and Plex Pass price hikes since 2024 have pushed many users to Jellyfin, and on Intel Quick Sync the experience is nearly identical. You can always run Plex alongside Jellyfin on any of the 8GB+ picks on this list to test both before committing. Whichever you choose, the best NAS for Jellyfin or Plex is the one with the Intel CPU that fits your budget and your library size.

Best Budget NAS for Plex and Jellyfin

Updated: October 9, 2026

Disclosure: GearSift is reader-supported. We research every pick, and no brand pays to be included. This article contains no affiliate links. How we make money

Want your own Netflix-style library at home? A NAS can store your movies and run Plex or Jellyfin to stream them to your TV, phone or laptop. The catch: when a device can’t play a file as-is, the server has to convert it on the fly (transcoding). That’s where cheap NAS boxes often struggle. Here’s what to look for, and three picks that fit.

How we chose: research-based. We compared manufacturer specifications with Plex’s and Jellyfin’s own hardware guidance and Intel’s processor specs (cited below, checked October 9, 2026). We have not physically tested these products.

Quick picks
Best budget pick: UGREEN NASync DXP2800. Intel N100, a processor Jellyfin names in its recommended list, plus 8 GB of RAM [1][5][7].
Step-up for bigger libraries: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus. Four bays, a 5-core Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with Quick Sync, and a 10GbE port [2][8].
If you want Synology’s software: Synology DS225+. Polished DSM apps, but older hardware for transcoding [3][9].
What matters for a media server

1. Intel Quick Sync. Plex’s hardware-accelerated streaming uses Intel Quick Sync Video on Intel systems [4]. Jellyfin supports Intel graphics through QSV and VA-API [6]. All three picks have Intel processors that Intel lists with Quick Sync Video [7][8][9].

2. Plex Pass vs Jellyfin. In Plex, hardware-accelerated streaming is a premium feature that needs an active Plex Pass subscription [4]. Jellyfin is free software, with no fees for the server or official clients [10].

3. A newer processor. Jellyfin’s hardware guide lists the Intel N100 among recommended processors for a server using integrated graphics. It also advises avoiding Intel J/M/N/Y-series low-power chips up to 11th gen when you’re buying [5].

4. Enough RAM. Jellyfin recommends at least 8 GB for an average setup (4 GB may be enough on a Linux server without a GUI) [5].

5. HEVC (H.265). Plex says NAS users need a Jasper Lake or better CPU to reliably transcode to HEVC output [4]. Jellyfin calls HEVC 10-bit hardware decoding the most important codec feature to look for [5].

Good to know: if your TV or streaming box can play your files directly (“Direct Play”), the NAS does far less work. UGREEN notes that Direct Play places relatively little demand on the NAS [2].

UGREEN NASync DXP2800: best budget pick

Who it’s for: a first media server for a household, with room for Docker apps.

Intel N100 with Quick Sync Video [7]. Jellyfin lists the N100 among its recommended processors for integrated-graphics servers [5].
8 GB DDR5, which meets Jellyfin’s 8 GB recommendation, upgradable to 16 GB [1][5].
UGREEN says it supports Docker and virtual machines, and that Plex can run in Docker [1]. Jellyfin publishes an official Docker image [6].
Two M.2 NVMe slots, a 2.5GbE port and 4K HDMI output [1].
UGREEN rates it at 16.38 W during drive access and 5.24 W in drive hibernation, measured in its own lab [1].
Watch out: two bays means RAID 1 at most for redundancy [1]. UGREEN lists it as diskless, so budget for drives [1].

UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: the step-up

Who it’s for: bigger libraries that need four drives and RAID 5/6, or a 10GbE desktop.

Intel Pentium Gold 8505, 5 cores / 6 threads, with Quick Sync Video [8].
UGREEN’s FAQ says you can run Plex in Docker, and that the 8505’s Quick Sync “can assist with compatible hardware-transcoding workloads.” It adds that Plex’s own hardware-transcoding requirements still apply [2].
4 SATA bays with RAID 5, 6 and 10, plus two M.2 NVMe slots [2].
8 GB DDR5, expandable to 64 GB [2].
10GbE + 2.5GbE ports [2]. UGREEN notes every part of the path (computer, switch, cabling, drives) must support 10GbE to get near those speeds [2].
Watch out: it draws more power: UGREEN rates it at 42.36 W during drive access and 18.12 W in hibernation (measured with a Seagate 2TB drive) [2]. It’s diskless [2].

See the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus on UGREEN

Synology DS225+: if you want Synology’s software

Who it’s for: people who value Synology’s DSM apps and a 3-year warranty, and who mostly Direct Play.

Intel Celeron J4125 [3], which Intel lists with Quick Sync Video and Intel UHD Graphics 600 [9].
Plex lists Synology among NAS platforms with Plex Media Server packages; you install it following the NAS maker’s add-on procedure [11].
Jellyfin’s Synology guide installs Jellyfin with Synology’s Container Manager (Docker) [12], and Synology lists the DS225+ as a supported Container Manager model [13].
Watch out, RAM: the DS225+ ships with 2 GB (max 6 GB) [3]. Jellyfin recommends allocating at least 4 GB of RAM to its container on Synology [12], so plan on a memory upgrade.
Watch out, processor age: Intel lists the J4125 as Gemini Lake Refresh, launched Q4 2019, and marks it discontinued [9]. Jellyfin doesn’t name the J4125, but it advises avoiding Intel J/M/N/Y-series low-power chips up to 11th gen when buying [5]. The J4125 is a 2019 J-series chip [9], an older generation than Jasper Lake, which Jellyfin’s Intel guide calls 10th Gen [6]. Applying that advice to the J4125 is our inference. Jellyfin’s Intel guide does list HEVC 10-bit decode and encode for Gemini Lake [6]. Plex says reliable HEVC-output transcoding on a NAS needs Jasper Lake or better [4], so check Plex’s NAS compatibility sheet before counting on it.

Setup tips
Use Ethernet. Jellyfin recommends a wired connection and says Wi-Fi or Powerline for the server will give a poor experience [5]. (Planned guide: Best 2.5GbE switches for a home network.)
Plex users: check you have Plex Pass before relying on hardware transcoding [4].
Keep a backup. Your media library is one copy. (Planned explainer: NAS vs DAS vs external hard drive.)
FAQ

Can the UniFi UNAS 2 run Plex or Jellyfin?
Ubiquiti’s spec page for the UNAS 2 doesn’t list third-party apps, and it uses an ARM processor [14]. If you want Plex or Jellyfin on the NAS itself, pick one of the Intel models above.

How many streams can these handle at once?
We couldn’t find an official stream count for any of these models, so we don’t give one. It depends on your files, your devices and your settings. UGREEN notes that transcoding demand varies with codec, resolution, bitrate, subtitles and client [2].

Do I need Plex Pass?
For Plex hardware-accelerated streaming, yes [4]. Jellyfin says there are no fees to use it [10].

 All four run containers: UGOS Pro Docker on UGREEN and DSM Container Manager on Synology. For hardware transcoding, choose the Intel Quick Sync path on the two UGREEN picks. Plex’s matrix currently marks both Synology models No for hardware transcoding.
 Sources: UGREEN DXP2800 , DXP4800 Plus , Synology DS225+ , DS925+ and the Plex NAS matrix . These are maker-supported memory ceilings.
 Two bays: start with DXP2800, or choose DSM
 Buy the DXP2800 when the first jobs are media, shared files and a few containers. Its N100 gives you the Intel graphics route for hardware transcoding, while the two NVMe slots leave your SATA bays available for a mirrored HDD pair.
 Buy the DS225+ when you want DSM’s backup workflow in the smaller enclosure. Its 2 GB starting RAM and 6 GB official ceiling are tighter limits for a growing application collection. Keep its main job focused.
 Our DXP2800 vs DS225+ comparison covers their apps, media differences and expansion in detail. The short version: UGREEN for the media project; Synology for the DSM workflow. 
 Four bays for movies and containers: DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus is the strongest fit here when you want the NAS to do several jobs: hold a growing movie library, run Docker applications and serve large files over a faster network. Four SATA bays give you more layout choices, and the 64 GB memory ceiling leaves more room for applications than either two-bay pick.
 UGREEN documents Intel Quick Sync support for its Pentium Gold 8505 in the NAS hardware guide . UGOS Pro supplies Docker and virtual-machine apps . Start with the installed 8 GB, watch memory use as you add services, then upgrade for a real workload.
 Choose DXP4800 Plus specifically: the plain DXP4800, GT and Pro are different models. This pick has one 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port. The 10GbE connection is useful for large transfers to a suitably equipped workstation or switch; you can still start on 2.5GbE.
 Four bays for DSM backups: DS925+
 Choose the DS925+ when the software is the attraction. Its four bays, 4 GB of ECC memory and 32 GB ceiling make it a more expandable DSM base than the DS225+. Both models support Container Manager , so choosing the backup-focused NAS does not mean giving up containers.
 Synology’s DS925+ datasheet describes Active Backup Suite for endpoint workloads, Hyper Backup for copying NAS data to another destination, and Snapshot Replication for versioned recovery. That is the appeal: a set of tools you can turn into a repeatable backup routine.
 Use it as a file store for a separate media mini PC if you want DSM and hardware transcoding together. For an all-in-one media box, choose the Intel UGREEN instead.
 Synology’s current drive policy: what changed
 Checked October 25, 2026: DSM 7.3 allows third-party HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs in new pools on 2025 DiskStation Plus models, including these two Synology picks. You are not limited to Synology-branded HDDs. Models on the explicit incompatibility list remain unsupported.
 The NVMe rule is narrower: new M.2 storage pools and SSD cache require drives on the compatibility list. Match the exact NAS and SSD before planning that upgrade. Synology’s drive-compatibility policy separates the drive types; old blanket claims about all third-party drives miss that distinction.
 How many bays do you actually need?
 Two bays suit a focused file collection that fits comfortably on one drive’s capacity, mirrored across a pair. Four bays make more sense when the collection is already growing or you want a parity layout without replacing both disks just to gain space.
 Here is the arithmetic for matched 8 TB drives , using nominal decimal capacity:
